scope: One broadclub cuttlefish for the species guide, isolated inspection and optional identification. The broad fin skirt, arm crown and distinctive pupils add a cephalopod comparison. No reef population or engine metadata is added.
iucnYearConvention: The current SeaLifeBase record reports global Data Deficient, assessed 15 March 2009. The year field uses that assessment date, not the 2012 publication year of the linked IUCN record. Data Deficient is not an assessment of low extinction risk.

specimens.name: Broadclub cuttlefish
marks: A broad oval mantle is edged by a thin, rippling fin skirt
Large eyes have W-shaped pupils and yellow along their lower edges
Eight short arms surround the mouth; two longer feeding tentacles tuck into pockets
Pale bands edge the arms, while cream and brown mottling varies across the body
specimens.role: A reef predator that catches small fish and crustaceans.
specimens.fact: Its appearance can change quickly. Colour cells and raised skin bumps help create different patterns and textures, so a single colour pattern is not a reliable identity check.
specimens.habitat: Shallow tropical coral reefs across the Indo-Pacific, from eastern Africa to the western Pacific and northern Australia.
specimens.behavior: Ripples its narrow fins to hover and move slowly. When catching prey, two longer tentacles reach out, then the eight arms hold and move the food toward the mouth.
specimens.observe: Trace the fin skirt around the mantle and look closely at a pupil. Compare the body outline with the day octopus, then use an underside view to find the rows of arm suckers.

claimSupport.acceptedName: WoRMS accepts Ascarosepion latimanus (Quoy & Gaimard, 1832), AphiaID 1667002. Sepia latimanus is the superseded combination used by older references and some recent research. Current genus list and indexed taxon details agree.
claimSupport.morphology: FAO describes an oval mantle, four rows of arm suckers, papillose skin, pale arm margins and a yellow lower eye border. Its tentacular clubs are crescent-shaped; those clubs remain retracted in this calm illustrated pose.
claimSupport.pupilAndPockets: The expert DORIS species account describes the W-shaped pupil with an anterior notch and two long tentacles stored in pockets among eight visible arms. Pupil appearance is illustrative, not a simulated light response. Its generic reproductive section conflicts with the species-specific FAO diagnosis and is not used.
claimSupport.feeding: Omura and Ikeda directly examined this species’ arm and tentacular suckers. Their abstract supports tentacle capture followed by arm handling. Aquarium husbandry information supports the fish, shrimp and crab diet and slow fin-driven movement.
claimSupport.variation: How et al. documented multiple hunting displays in wild animals, differing in posture, colour and texture. The mottled model represents one quiet appearance; neither its palette nor its pose is a universal identifier. No claim that prey are literally hypnotized is introduced.
claimSupport.rangeAndDepth: FAO gives tropical Indo-Pacific reefs to 30 m. DORIS documents a 5 m observation in New Caledonia. The model-reference interval [5,30] is a conservative display reference, not an exhaustive depth range or physiological limit.
claimSupport.size: Nominal .30 m means the full posed mantle, head and arm crown, with retracted tentacles; it is not mantle length, a typical adult size or a maximum. FAO reports a maximum of 500 mm mantle length. The model mantle is approximately .18–.20 m; source measurements must not be compared directly with posed total length.
claimSupport.conservation: SeaLifeBase’s current global IUCN field reports DD and 15 March 2009. Direct IUCN access was unavailable, so no unreviewed rationale, population trend or new assessment is inferred.
claimSupport.comparison: The one-way day_octopus link teaches the fin-edged mantle and arm arrangement by contrasting two existing guide forms. It is an educational comparison, not a closest-relative or field-identification key claim.

specimens.caution: The model is an illustrative unsexed animal, not a complete identification key. It does not simulate chromatophore control, prey capture, jetting or an adaptive pupil. The feeding tentacles remain retracted in the calm pose; their capture clubs are not permanently exposed. No sex, lifespan, toxicity, handling or aquarium-care claims are introduced.

modelProvenance.lengthMeaning: Full posed mantle, head and arm crown with feeding tentacles retracted; not mantle length, typical size or maximum
modelProvenance.palette: Illustrative cream and brown mottling, pale arm/fin margins and yellow lower eye rims; unsexed, without a male-specific breeding display
modelProvenance.motion: Gentle local fin ripples and small arm movement around a fixed root; no locomotion or prey-capture sequence
modelProvenance.hostContext: Isolated reef-associated cephalopod with no added reef population or encounter
